subject: chemistry
question_text: Define dipole moment and write its applications.

verification.note: Chapter 3 is sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack chemistry section (book pp.56-61), which prints the question, its star rank and a model answer. Only ONE source book is held for chemistry — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only — so the two-book union check is PENDING a second chemistry source. The 1+1+1+1 mark split is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. Dipole moment appears TWICE in the book's SAQ list — this applications form (SAQ 8) and a why-is-BF₃-zero form (SAQ 9). They share only the definition and differ in focus at the same length, so they are authored as two separate cards, not as cuts of one.

steps.label: Definition
lines: Dipole moment (μ): the product of the
magnitude of the charge on either pole and
the distance between the two poles of a
steps.why: A polar molecule is two opposite partial charges a fixed distance apart, so its polarity is measured by the product of that charge and that distance.
common_mistakes: Leaving out the word product and writing a sum or a ratio.
Forgetting that μ is a vector — direction matters when moments are added.
steps.memory_tip: Two poles: charge times the distance between them.
steps.margin_note: Definition in words plus the equation μ = δ × d earns the full mark.

steps.label: Units
lines: debye (D), and the SI unit coulomb metre
steps.why: Charge in coulomb times distance in metre gives coulomb metre; the debye is the practical unit sized for molecules, so both units and the conversion are expected.
common_mistakes: Writing coulomb per metre. The unit is coulomb TIMES metre (C·m).
Misplacing the power of ten in the conversion: it is 10⁻³⁰.
steps.memory_tip: Charge unit times distance unit: coulomb metre. Debye is its molecule-sized version.
steps.margin_note: The 1 D conversion value is also asked alone as a very short answer.

steps.label: Polar or non-polar test
lines: If μ = 0, the compound is non-polar.
If μ ≠ 0, the compound is polar.
Ex: μ of BF₃ is zero (non-polar);
μ of NH₃ is not zero (polar).
steps.why: The measured moment is the direct test of molecular polarity: a symmetric molecule's bond moments cancel to zero even when its individual bonds are polar.
common_mistakes: Concluding non-polar bonds from μ = 0. The BONDS can be polar while the MOLECULE is non-polar by symmetry.
steps.memory_tip: Zero moment, non-polar molecule; any non-zero moment, polar molecule.
steps.margin_note: One example on each side of the test reads best.

steps.label: Percentage ionic character
lines: Observed μ is the measured value;
calculated μ assumes a fully ionic bond.
steps.why: Comparing the measured moment with the value a 100% ionic bond would give tells how far the real bond is toward ionic — the ratio scaled to a percentage.
common_mistakes: Inverting the ratio. The observed (measured) value goes on top.
Not saying what the calculated value means: the fully ionic assumption.
steps.memory_tip: Real value over ideal ionic value, times 100.
steps.margin_note: Say in words what observed and calculated mean under the boxed formula.

insider_note: Two marks sit in the definition with its equation and units line — and the 1 D conversion value is regularly asked on its own, so it must be exact.
